n: People make plans in their hearts, but the final word belongs to the Lord. Several verses in this chapter explore how human planning and God’s guidance work together.

f.g: The plans or arrangements of the mind.

n: We tend to think all our actions are fine, but the Lord weighs our motives. He sees what lies beneath the surface.
Entrust your work to the Lord, and your plans will succeed. Literally, “roll” your works onto him.

f.g: Literally “roll”—roll your burden onto the Lord.

n: The Lord has a purpose for everything, and even the wicked will meet their day of judgment. This doesn’t mean God makes people wicked; it means no one escapes his justice.

f.g: Or “for its purpose / its answer.”
The day of calamity or judgment.

n: The Lord detests the proud; be sure of it, they will not go unpunished.

f.g: Possibly “be assured” (a pledge by handshake).

n: Steadfast love and faithfulness atone for sin, and reverence for the Lord leads people away from evil. Latter-day Saints see ultimate atonement in Christ, whose mercy and truth meet.

f.g: purged = atoned for, covered.

n: When a person’s ways please God, he can make even enemies live at peace with them—as with Jacob and Esau.

f.w: his enemies to be at peace with him

n: Better a little gained honestly than great income gained unjustly.

f.w: Better is a little with righteousness

n: We plan our route, but the Lord guides our steps. Make plans—but stay open to his direction.
An ideal: a king speaks with God-given authority and should not betray justice. Verses 10–15 describe what a righteous king should be.

f.g: An inspired decision, almost like an oracle.

n: Honest scales and weights belong to the Lord. Fair business is his concern too.

f.w: all the weights of the bag
f.g: Merchants carried stone weights in a pouch for weighing silver.

n: Kings should detest wrongdoing, because a throne stands firm on righteousness.

f.w: the throne is established by righteousness

n: Good rulers value honest advisers and those who speak the truth.
A king’s anger can mean death, but a wise person will calm it.

f.g: pacify = calm, appease.

n: The king’s favor is life-giving, like the spring rain clouds that ripen the harvest.

f.w: a cloud of the latter rain
f.g: The spring rains (March–April) that matured crops before harvest.

n: Getting wisdom is far better than getting gold, and understanding is better than silver.

f.w: How much better is it to get wisdom than gold

n: The highway of the upright avoids evil; whoever watches his path guards his life.

f.g: A raised, cleared road—a straight, well-made path.

n: Perhaps the best-known proverb: pride comes before disaster and arrogance before a fall. The Book of Mormon’s “pride cycle” illustrates it repeatedly.

f.g: haughty = arrogant, lofty.

n: Better to be humble among the poor than to share loot with the proud.

f.g: Share the plunder after battle.

n: Paying attention to instruction brings good results, and trusting the Lord brings true happiness.

f.w: whoso trusteth in the LORD, happy is he

n: The wise are recognized as discerning, and pleasant speech makes teaching more persuasive.

f.w: the sweetness of the lips increaseth learning
f.g: Gracious speech makes instruction more persuasive.

n: Understanding is a fountain of life to its owner; fools are disciplined by their own folly.

f.g: wellspring = a fountain, source of water.

n: A wise heart guides the mouth and makes speech persuasive.

f.w: The heart of the wise teacheth his mouth

n: Kind words are like honey—sweet to the soul and healing to the body.

f.g: Healing for the whole body.

n: This repeats 14:12 word for word: a path can seem right yet lead to death. The repetition emphasizes how easily we deceive ourselves.

f.w: There is a way that seemeth right unto a man

n: Hunger motivates a worker; his appetite drives him on. Need can be a healthy spur to labor.

f.w: his mouth craveth it of him
f.g: His hunger urges him on.

n: A worthless person digs up trouble like someone digging a pit, and his words burn like fire.

f.g: Hebrew “man of belial”—a worthless scoundrel.

n: A perverse person spreads conflict, and a gossip separates close friends.

f.g: whisperer = gossip, slanderer.
Close, intimate friends.

n: A violent person lures a neighbor into wrongdoing. Evil often recruits.
Squinting eyes and pursed lips—body language of someone plotting harm.

f.g: Winks or narrows his eyes, a sign of scheming.

n: Gray hair is a crown of glory when it comes through a righteous life. Old age lived well is honorable.

f.g: hoary = gray or white with age.

n: Self-control is greater than military might. Ruling your own temper is harder than conquering a city.
Lots—like dice—were thrown into a fold of the garment to make decisions, but the outcome is in God’s hands. Nothing is mere chance to him.

f.w: The lot is cast into the lap
f.g: Casting lots was a common way of making decisions in Israel.
